scenes.narration: October 1973. OPEC's oil embargo slams into the American economy like a sledgehammer. Gas lines stretch around the block. And economists watch something impossible unfold: prices soaring while jobs disappear. The word 'stagflation' is about to enter the dictionary.
scenes.visual_prompt: Black and white news footage of long gas station lines in 1973 America, cars stretching around the block, anxious drivers, sepia tone.

scenes.narration: For thirty years, Keynesian economics had promised a tradeoff: you could have inflation or unemployment, but not both. The Phillips curve was gospel. Then in 1973 the curve broke. And the entire profession had to admit a humbling truth: the models were wrong.
scenes.visual_prompt: Archival footage of economists at a Federal Reserve meeting, grainy, concerned expressions, papers shuffling, 1970s aesthetic.

scenes.narration: Milton Friedman had warned this was coming. His 1967 address predicted that any attempt to exploit the Phillips curve long-term would cause exactly what America was now experiencing: accelerating inflation with no lasting employment gains. Six years later, reality proved him right.
scenes.visual_prompt: Milton Friedman at a University of Chicago lectern, wire-rimmed glasses, 1967 black-and-white photography, academic intensity.
